unintended_consequences: Observed in China: (a) stimulus that pulls demand forward creates cliffs — home-appliance sales fell 8.7% and autos 16.1% in June 2026 as trade-in subsidies rolled off, so the policy bought volume from the future rather than creating it; (b) the anti-involution campaign intended to protect producers risks protecting incumbents and raising consumer prices in an already weak-demand economy, and analysts widely doubt it can end deflation without capacity cuts that would themselves cause layoffs; (c) frugality became identity rather than constraint — 反向消费 is now performed as intelligence and taste, meaning consumption may not recover proportionally even if incomes do, a permanent preference shift that no stimulus can address; (d) the downgrade produced world-beating export champions by accident — Mixue, Pop Mart, Miniso, Luckin, Temu and Shein are all products of a domestic market that forced extreme cost discipline, and they are now conquering Southeast Asia; China's consumer weakness became China's consumer-brand strength abroad; (e) the emotional economy grew precisely because the material economy shrank, creating a RMB 2.3 trillion sector out of anxiety; (f) the civil-service exam absorbed a generation's ambition, a human-capital misallocation with a decades-long tail; (g) the deepest downgrade occurred in the richest cities, inverting the expected pattern and hollowing out exactly the Tier-1 consumer base that global brands had built their China strategies around. Predicted for Indonesia: (a) the Temu block intended to protect MSMEs simply routed cheap Chinese goods through Shopee and TikTok Shop cross-border listings and grey channels instead — protection without a domestic supply alternative displaces the flow rather than stopping it; (b) demand stimulus (transport discounts, electricity subsidies, food aid) may entrench expectations of subsidy while leaving job quality untouched, making each subsequent package politically necessary and economically less effective; (c) the value-retail boom may create more retail jobs than it destroys while lowering average retail wages, so employment statistics improve as living standards fall; (d) down-trading could inadvertently build Indonesia's first genuine national discount-retail infrastructure — a durable, efficiency-improving legacy of a painful period, exactly as China's did; (e) Chinese value chains entering to serve Indonesian downgrade may crowd out the domestic value operators who would otherwise have emerged, so Indonesia gets the format without the ownership; (f) rising second-hand, repair and rental economies could deliver a genuine sustainability dividend nobody planned; (g) the same social-media dynamic driving frugality culture also drives doom spending and blind-box mania, so Indonesia may end up with China's frugality AND a more severe version of China's compulsive-spending problem, because it lacks the regulatory and savings buffers China had; (h) if Gen Z's frugality persists into their peak earning years, Indonesia's demographic-dividend consumption boom — the core assumption behind a decade of retail and FMCG investment — may simply never arrive.
kelompok_rentan: (1) The lower-middle class and 'aspiring middle class' (137.5 million people, 49.22% of the population) — the cohort with just enough income to have adopted middle-class consumption commitments (motorcycle instalments, private schooling, BPJS top-ups, digital subscriptions) and no buffer to sustain them; this is where the 9.48 million who dropped out came from. (2) Gen Z and young workers — 34% carrying P2P/online-loan exposure, entering a labour market with contracting real wages and degraded job quality, and the group most exposed to doom spending, blind-box mechanics and status-anxiety consumption. (3) Textile, garment and footwear workers — the epicentre of Indonesian layoffs and the direct casualties of import-driven down-trading. (4) Warung owners and traditional market traders — losing volume to minimarket and value-chain formats while their own household finances deteriorate; they are simultaneously displaced producers and stressed consumers. (5) Retail and F&B workers in mid-market and premium formats — hypermarket employees (336 to 244 outlets, Lulu's exit), department-store staff, casual-dining crew. (6) Regional distributors and sales agents outside Java — the first cost line cut when brand principals fund price competition, and a major source of formal non-Java employment. (7) Small domestic manufacturers and convection workshops — unable to match imported price points and unable to access modern-trade shelves without certification they cannot afford. (8) Non-Java consumers generally — trading down while paying a freight premium and receiving less format choice. (9) Fresh graduates — entering a market where the graduate premium is compressing and where, as in China, the rational response is to queue for CPNS/PPPK rather than produce. (10) Households dependent on commodity-cycle regional economies, whose incomes swing hardest. (11) Children and adolescents — exposed to gambling-adjacent blind-box and gacha mechanics that Indonesia, unlike China since 2023, does not regulate.
kasus_china: (1) Mixue Bingcheng (蜜雪冰城) — the definitive downgrade-era business model. Drinks at RMB 4-8, profit made on supply-chain margin to franchisees rather than on retail margin, scaled to become the world's largest F&B chain by outlet count and then exported wholesale to Southeast Asia, reaching ~2,600 Indonesian outlets by end-2025. It proves that in a trading-down economy the winning structure is supply-chain ownership plus franchise density, not brand premium. (2) The snack-collection duopoly — 鸣鸣很忙 (零食很忙 + 赵一鸣零食) and 万辰集团 (好想来), each at roughly 15,000-20,000 stores, having built a national retail format from nothing in about five years by stripping brand rent out of the snack category; the discount-store channel grew 92% YoY and snack-collection stores 51%. (3) Pinduoduo — the origin case: NASDAQ IPO in July 2018 just 2 years 11 months after founding, the RMB 10 billion subsidy programme from June 2019, and continued +11% growth in Q1 2025 when the rest of e-commerce stalled; PDD made 'cheap' respectable and forced Alibaba and JD to build their own value channels. (4) The RMB 9.9 coffee war — Luckin versus Cotti through 2023-2024, which reset China's entire coffee price expectation downward and destroyed the mid-tier café segment, a direct preview of Indonesia's sub-Rp 20,000 coffee war. (5) The 2024 food-service extinction event — nearly 3 million establishments closed, over half of Shanghai's high-end restaurants gone, Michelin-starred venues failing within months of opening; the clearest measure of how fast premium consumption capacity can disappear. (6) Beijing and Shanghai cosmetics -26.4% YoY in 2024 alongside Bain's -20% luxury contraction — evidence that the downgrade hit hardest at the top, inverting the usual assumption that value-seeking starts at the bottom. (7) Pop Mart / Labubu — the counter-case and the paradox: revenue RMB 37.12 billion in 2025 (+185%), The Monsters IP +668% YoY in H1 2025, one figure auctioned for RMB 1.08 million, the stock up ~200% then down ~40% from its August peak. Affective consumption boomed precisely as material consumption contracted, and then proved fragile — the lipstick effect at national scale, with a warning attached. (8) The 2026 civil-service exam — 3.72 million qualified applicants for about 38,100 posts; the human-capital cost of a low-margin private economy. (9) November 2025's +1.3% retail print and the -13.1% industrial-profit fall in the same month — the two numbers that together define the wage-margin-consumption doom loop and that triggered the elevation of consumption in the 15th Five-Year Plan.
padanan_indonesia: (1) MR.DIY Indonesia — the closest structural analogue to China's hard-discount formats and the clearest proof of format-market fit: 1,200th store in December 2025, 1,278 in Q1 2026, 1,349 by H1 2026, Q1 2026 revenue IDR 2.4 trillion (+31.0% YoY) with PAT +35.5%, achieved in the same months that national retail sales fell 3.7-3.9% YoY. A discounter growing 31% while the market contracts 4% is the textbook signature of a trading-down economy. (2) Mixue Indonesia — the direct import of the Chinese downgrade playbook: entered 2020, ~2,600 outlets by end-2025, then began streamlining as the market saturated; Indonesia compressed China's five-year value-beverage cycle into roughly the same span. (3) Cigarette down-trading — the cleanest quantitative Indonesian evidence: Group I (highest excise) production -10%, Group II +1.3%, Group III +7%, with total output at 307.9 billion sticks in 2025, the lowest in years, plus rising illicit prevalence. Excise policy inadvertently built the down-trading ladder. (4) The hypermarket-to-minimarket migration — hypermarkets from 336 (2019) to 244 (2024) with Lulu exiting on 30 April 2025, while Indomaret and Alfamart reached 44,366 combined outlets; Indonesia's version of China's channel migration, though toward proximity-convenience rather than toward hard discount. (5) Alfamart's earnings as the middle-class barometer — net income -7% in 2024 and -3.5% YoY in 9M 2025, with RTD beverage sales down about 20%: the discretionary top-up purchase is the first casualty. (6) The BPS middle-class series — 57.33 million (2019) to 46.7 million (2025), 9.48 million people dropping out; Indonesia's structural equivalent of China's property-wealth shock, arriving through the labour market instead. (7) Promotion dependence — 39% of cooking-oil purchases promotion-driven in 2024, up from 22% in 2022; the Indonesian analogue of China's 87.1% value-first consumers. (8) The Labubu queues, sold-out concerts and strong iPhone demand alongside falling retail sales — Indonesia's version of the emotional-upgrade paradox, explicitly discussed domestically as doom spending and the lipstick effect, with beauty's +16% value growth in 2024 as the measurable carve-out. (9) The October 2024 Temu block — Indonesia's structural divergence from China: with no domestic white-label base, the state blocks the value supply rather than absorbing it, which is the single most consequential difference between the two trajectories. (10) Chagee's April 2025 PIK Avenue launch via an Erajaya JV with pre-secured halal certification — the template for how Chinese value formats will actually enter: licensed, partnered and certified, not cross-border and unmediated.

catatan_kontradiksi_data: (1) The 'downgrade' label is contested. Bain, Premia Partners and Baiguan all argue that China is not simply consuming less but consuming differently — volume rose +4.4% in 2024 even as ASP fell -3.4%, and services retail (+5.3% in H1 2026) far outpaced goods (+1.1%). Xinhua's official position explicitly disputes the downgrade framing. Both readings are supportable; the honest description is 'volume-preserving, price-destroying re-composition', not a demand collapse. (2) Indonesian middle-class figures diverge by definition. BPS uses the World Bank 3.5-17x poverty-line expenditure band and reports 47.85 million (2024) / 46.7 million (2025); other analysts using different income cutoffs report larger middle classes and milder declines, and some (including FULCRUM/ISEAS) argue the 'shrinking middle class' narrative overstates the case because the aspiring middle class grew simultaneously. The direction is unambiguous; the magnitude is not. (3) Indonesian headline growth contradicts consumer data. Q1 2026 GDP printed 5.61% — the highest since 2022 — while retail sales fell 3.7-3.9% YoY in April-May 2026, consumer confidence hit a nine-month low, and real wages contracted in the largest employing sectors. Government and critical analysts read these facts oppositely; the discrepancy likely reflects government-consumption and investment contributions masking household weakness. (4) China's November 2025 retail figure is variously cited at +1.3% (TrendForce, CNBC, SCMP) and as an eight-month or three-year low depending on the series used (goods only versus goods-and-services, and whether services retail is included); Chinese statistical practice changed in 2025 to headline 'goods and services retail', which makes year-on-year comparisons with pre-2025 series unreliable. (5) The H1 2026 figure of +1.3% for consumer-goods retail sits alongside +2.7% for goods-and-services retail — these are different aggregates and are frequently conflated in secondary reporting. (6) Layoff counts for Indonesia vary widely: Kemnaker recorded 88,519 for 2025 while mid-2025 reporting cited about 70,000 by that point and unions claim substantially higher figures; official counts capture only formally reported terminations and systematically understate informal-sector job loss. (7) Pop Mart's trajectory is contradictory within a single year: revenue +185% in 2025 with the stock up ~200%, then a ~40% drawdown from the August peak and a 22% single-day plunge in March 2026 — the emotional economy is real but its durability is unproven, so any Indonesian forecast built on it is fragile. (8) Mixue's Indonesian store count (~2,600 at end-2025) is followed by reports of outlet streamlining in Indonesia and Vietnam during the subsequent half-year, so the expansion narrative and the saturation narrative are both currently true and depend on the reference date. (9) China's programme-withdrawal counts in the MOE major-optimisation cycle differ by source (figures around 1,700 for 2024 are commonly cited but not consistently sourced), so the education-response section is marked uncertain. (10) The lag framing itself is contestable for this domain: Indonesia's middle-class contraction began in 2019, before China's structural downgrade (2021-2022), so on the pure demand dimension Indonesia may be leading rather than lagging — the lag is genuine only on the supply-side infrastructure and policy-response dimensions. (11) Indonesian FMCG data show simultaneous downtrading (baby care, beverages, dairy, home care) and premiumisation (beauty +16% in 2024), which some analysts, including Bain's 2026 outlook, read as evidence that Indonesia is premiumising rather than trading down; the reconciliation is category polarisation, not a contradiction, but headline claims in either direction are unreliable.
